rows.title: No picture
rows.text: Nobody has recorded an eye type for you. Nobody has measured whether any part of you forms an image of what is around you.
rows.note: R1 covers moth and beetle eyes only, so I did not cite it. I left out "you have no eyes" and any light-sensing claim because no plant record supports them.

rows.title: Neighbors
rows.text: If you are a wood strawberry, your daughter plants grow more root over live substrate than over dead substrate, so you detect the state of a patch before you touch it. You also sense red and far-red light through a protein called phytochrome B. For nearly every other plant that borrows this row, nobody has measured whether you sense your neighbors by chemicals or by light.
rows.note: Left out common dandelion's R1 (airborne volatiles from damaged neighbors): its quote gives no result. Far-red records for selfheal (R5) not tied to neighbors.

rows.title: Green and time
rows.text: You have no eyes, and for most plants nobody has measured how you sense light or what you do at each hour of the day. A few have been measured: common selfheal grows less under strong far-red light, English plantain grows larger under added ultraviolet-B, and Queen Anne's lace makes chlorophyll according to day length. For the hour of the day, chicory is one that has been measured, and its flower heads begin to open around sunrise.
rows.note: No record covers how plants sense green light, so the row says nothing about green. Black locust, also measured for both traits, was left out for length.
